1:
The chapter opens with the two voices that broke a long silence, and the witnesses gather first around the men and the moment. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the scene: in the second year of Darius Hystaspis the prophets Haggai and Zechariah arose and exhorted the people, by words both of reproof and of encouragement, to take up again the work of rebuilding the house of God; and it was in consequence of these prophetic admonitions that the rulers of the community resumed the building. On the vexed patronymic — Zechariah "the son of Iddo" — the reformed John Gill, the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, and John Wesley speak with one voice: he was strictly the grandson of Iddo, for his father was Berechiah, as his own prophecy declares in Zechariah 1:1.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supplies the history the bare notice presumes. The building had been suspended, he reckons, for as much as fifteen years; through that time the people had an altar and a tabernacle and made use of them, for when we cannot do what we would we must do what we can in the service of God. The counsellors hired to hinder the work had told them, perhaps with a pretence of inspiration, that the time was not yet come to build — the very complaint answered in Haggai 1:2 — and so the people were made easy in their own ceiled houses while God's house lay waste. Now, says Henry, life was put into a good cause that seemed to lie dead. Both prophets began in the second year of Darius, as Haggai 1:1 and Zechariah 1:1 attest; and the temple of God among men, he insists, is to be built by prophecy and not by secular force, for the instruments of our building, like the weapons of our warfare, are not carnal but spiritual. It is the business of God's prophets to stir up his people to their duty and to strengthen their hands, and it is a sign that God has mercy in store for a people when he raises up such helpers among them.

Henry lingers on the odd Hebrew of the address — they prophesied "unto them, upon them, even upon them" — comparing it to Ezekiel prophesying upon the dry bones that they might live in Ezekiel 37:4; with bishop Patrick he hears in it a note of rebuke, for the prophets reproved the people that they did not build. Wesley draws the whole to a point: the prophets came commanding them from God to return to the building of the temple, and they came with a promise of his favour and assistance.
2:
With the prophets' word ringing, the two leaders act, and the witnesses weigh both the spur behind them and the company that stood with them. The reformed John Gill reads the rising of Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak as an inward work before it was an outward one: their spirits were stirred up and quickened by the ministry of the prophets, the Lord himself accompanying that ministry by his good Spirit. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the chronology with care. To "begin to build" here is to take up the building properly so called upon the foundations already laid in Ezra 3:10; and they trace the very days of it — Haggai entered on his work the first day of the sixth month in the second year of Darius, and his first address made so deep an impression that Zerubbabel and Joshua, with the people, set about the long-intermitted work as early as the twenty-fourth day of that same month.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out the dignity of the alliance at work in the verse. Here three classes of men join in one sacred labour: Zerubbabel the civil governor, Jeshua the high priest or ecclesiastical governor, and Haggai and Zechariah the prophets. "How glorious it is," he exclaims, "when we see the civil government joining with the sacerdotal and prophetic for the establishment and extension of true religion!" Wesley agrees that the prophets' part was to help by encouraging the people to work, by their very presence and by their assurance of success; and he notes, with Clarke, that the work had stood still for about fifteen years, adding that the first chapter of Haggai is the best comment on these two verses.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott guards the verse against a false inference. "Then rose up" does not intimate that the leaders had grown indifferent and needed rousing from sloth; rather the voice of prophecy inspirited them to go forward without waiting for any formal permission from Darius — a king already known secretly to favour them. And in the two prophets who were "helping them," Ellicott says, we may read the invigorating sayings that encouraged the people almost from day to day and from stage to stage of their work. The witnesses do not divide. Together they show a leadership moved from within by the Spirit and from without by the word, the prince and the priest and the prophets bound in a single enterprise, and the whole recovery of the ruined house springing not from a royal decree newly obtained but from the preaching that God had lately sent.
3:
No sooner had the work revived than opposition revived with it, and the witnesses read the arrival of Tatnai as both a political fact and a spiritual pattern. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry catches the timing: a jealous eye was kept upon the builders, and no sooner did the Spirit of God stir up the friends of the temple than the evil spirit stirred up its enemies against it. He notes the pointed contrast — while the people had been content to build and panel their own houses the adversaries let them alone, as Haggai 1:4 observes, though the standing royal order to stop the building of the city was already on record in Ezra 4:21; but the moment they fell to work again on the temple, the alarm was taken. Yet Henry finds these particular enemies of a better temper than the former set: Tatnai and Shethar-boznai were men who made some conscience of telling the truth, for the church's enemies are not all equally wicked and unreasonable.

The reformed John Gill and John Wesley account for the new faces. These were fresh governors and officers set over the province, the old ones — Rehum and Shimshai and their company — being by now either dead or removed from office at the accession of the new king. The grammatical-historical witnesses fix Tatnai's rank and reach. Keil and Delitzsch make him the Pecha, the viceroy over the provinces west of the Euphrates, that is over Syria and Phoenicia, to which Judaea with its own Pecha Zerubbabel was subordinate; Shethar-Boznai they take for his secretary, and their "companions" for their subordinates. Charles Ellicott agrees, calling Tatnai the Satrap of the whole province of Syria and Phoenicia, with jurisdiction over Judaea and over Zerubbabel its sub-Satrap, and reckoning Shethar-boznai to Tatnai what Shimshai had been to Rehum.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the man's character from his conduct: governor of the provinces on that side of the Euphrates — Syria, Arabia Deserta, Phoenicia, and Samaria — Tatnai seems to have been mild and judicious, acting with great prudence and caution and without any prejudice, as the very manner of his report to the king would prove. Ellicott adds the reason the builders dared proceed under his questioning: the recent overthrow of Smerdis, the Magian usurper who had hated the religion of Zoroaster and destroyed temples, had emboldened them to go on without fear of the court of Darius; the two prophets had made their duty too plain to be deferred; and yet, he cautions, the decree of the preceding chapter had never been expressly revoked. So the officials' question — "Who hath commanded you to build this house?" — falls into a real legal uncertainty, and the whole chapter turns on how it will be answered.
4:
A small textual tangle hangs over this verse, and the witnesses spend their strength untangling it. The question is who is speaking — "Then said we unto them after this manner, What are the names of the men that make this building?" The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch settle it on the pronoun: from the word "we said" it is plain that the author of the account was himself an eye-witness of, and a sharer in, the work of building, so that the speakers are the Jews, not the officials. They grant that the answer here seems at first not to correspond with the question in the previous verse — the officials had asked who commanded the work, and the reply gives the names of the builders — but they explain the mismatch as the effect of compression, the whole exchange being reported only in a short extract restricted to its chief points.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse the same way and would render it without any interrogation at all: this is the Jews' answer to Tatnai's inquiry, and the sense is simply, "These are the names of the men who make this building." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott concurs. He knows that the Septuagint must have read "then said they," but he sees no need to alter the Hebrew: the clause is not a question but a statement — "we told them what the names were." And he notes what the compressed report leaves implicit, to be gathered from the tenth verse below: the authorities demanded the names of the chief promoters of the building precisely in order to fix responsibility upon them, should the enterprise prove unlawful.

The reformed John Gill canvasses the same options more warily. He records that some — Aben Ezra among them — take the words for those of the builders, others for those of the scribes or secretaries who came to question them, and one reading even assigns them to Tatnai's party; but he lands where the rest do, that they are the words of the Jews, since order requires it and otherwise no answer would be returned at all. Beneath the grammar the witnesses agree on the substance: the officials wanted names, the builders gave them, and the men who had dared to raise the house of God were content to be known and, if need be, held answerable for it. There is a quiet courage in the exchange, a people neither hiding their leaders nor disowning their work, but standing openly by both, and letting their very names go up in the record that would travel to the throne.
5:
Here the historian lifts his eyes from the officials to the providence that stood behind the builders, and the witnesses dwell on that watching eye. The reformed John Gill takes "the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews" as the language of favour: God looked graciously upon them, smiled on their work, encouraged them by his good Spirit and by the prophets, gave them success, and protected and defended them from their enemies. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the same thought at length and in two directions. The eye of God upon the elders who were active in the work meant, first, that their enemies could not cause them to cease, as they would gladly have done — for the officials asked only that the building might halt until instructions came from the king, and even that small concession the builders would not grant them. God's eye upon his servants baffled and enfeebled their adversaries and shielded the workmen from every malicious design; while we are employed in God's work, Henry says, we are taken under his special protection, and there are, as the prophet saw, seven eyes upon one stone in his temple, in Zechariah 3:9 and Zechariah 4:10.

But the eye of God, Henry adds, did more than defend; it also quickened. The elders of the Jews saw that eye upon them, to observe what they did and to own them in what they did well, and the sight gave them courage enough to face their enemies and to press on with the work in spite of all opposition. Our eye upon God, observing his eye upon us, will keep us to our duty and hearten us in it when the difficulties are most discouraging. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke says the same more briefly: the watchful care of God was upon the elders, who were assured of his favour and found his especial providence working in their behalf.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the grammar and the reach of that providence. Keil and Delitzsch stress that Tatnai had the power to prohibit the work outright, yet allowed it to go on until an answer should arrive from the king — and in this forbearance the historian sees the hand of God guarding the building. They correct a mistaken rendering that would make the clause read "until the command of Darius should arrive," showing that it speaks rather of the time until the matter came before him. Charles Ellicott presses the point further: the divine eye was fixed with special vigilance on the work, and its influence lay upon the Persian officials no less than upon the rulers of the Jews — as the fair and favourable letter that follows will plainly show.
6:
The narrative pauses to introduce the document itself, and the witnesses turn from the scene at Jerusalem to the letter that would carry the whole question to the throne. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the structure: verses six and seven form the superscription of the letter that the royal officials sent to Darius, answering in the second half of the book to the hostile letter of the Samaritans in Ezra 4:9 and following. The senders are Tatnai, Shethar-Boznai, and their "companions the Apharsachites," whom Keil identifies with the Apharsathchites named in the earlier chapter — a people, he suggests, specially devoted to the Persian king, holding a prominent place among the settlers of Syria, and perhaps forming the royal garrison there. The salutation itself he weighs: "To King Darius, much peace," or, taking the Aramaic strictly, peace "in all things," in every respect.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott seizes on the contrast between this letter and its predecessor. Tatnai's despatch is introduced much in the same way as the earlier accusation had been in the previous chapter, yet its whole temper is different: its dispassionateness and good faith stand in striking contrast to the malice of that former letter. Here is no attempt to inflame the king, but a fair and measured report. On the identity of the Apharsachites Ellicott is more cautious than confident, taking them for the same as the Apharsites mentioned before and suspecting them to be some kind of Persian guard, while frankly admitting that the reason for naming them specifically at this point is obscure.

The reformed John Gill canvasses the same name without pretending to certainty. Some, he notes, would make the Apharsachites one of the transplanted nations listed earlier, the word standing near to two of those names; but he thinks it may rather have been a distinct colony settled in the parts over which Tatnai bore rule. The witnesses do not contend. What they draw out together is the character of the moment: the same machinery of imperial correspondence that had once been turned against the Jews in an earlier reign is now set in motion by officials who mean them no harm, and the letter about to be quoted will lay the builders' case before the king with a candour their enemies had never shown. The very form of the thing — a formal report, courteously addressed, wishing the king peace in all things — signals that the tide at court has turned, and that the God whose eye was on the elders has bent even the imperial post to their good.
7:
The letter proper begins, and its first words are a wish of peace: "Unto Darius the king, all peace." The reformed John Gill notes only that this was the inscription of the letter, the customary superscription with which such a despatch to a sovereign would open. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch dwell a moment on the greeting, reading the Aramaic as a wish of peace "in all things" — peace to the king in every respect — and treating it as the courteous opening of a document that will then pass at once to a plain statement of the state of affairs. There is no flattery here and no venom; the officials salute the king and proceed to their report.

That plainness is itself the thing the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry most admires in the whole letter. Setting this despatch beside the venomous accusation an earlier set of adversaries had sent in a former reign, he marvels how fairly these men represented the matter to the king: they told him truly what was being done, they fully set out the Jews' own plea, and they were willing that the cause should be laid in a true light and fairly heard, leaving the king himself to judge. It is enough, Henry observes, if the cause of God and truth be fairly stated and fairly heard, for then it will keep its ground; the mischief comes only when it is misrepresented.

So the witnesses, few as they are on this bare verse of address, agree in reading the superscription as the token of a changed climate. The last letter written to a Persian king about these builders had been a piece of malice designed to procure a stoppage; this one opens with a wish of peace and will go on to state the facts without colouring them. The Jews' enemies in the former reign had prevailed only by misrepresentation; here the very form of the letter — its calm salutation, its evident willingness to let the truth appear — promises the builders a hearing they had been denied before. Gill's small point about the inscription and Keil's about the greeting thus open onto Henry's larger one: a fairly stated cause is already half won, and the God who had set his eye upon the elders has now inclined even the imperial correspondence in their favour. What begins with a courteous "all peace" will end, as the chapter and the next will show, in the peace of a house at last permitted to rise.
8:
The letter's opening report — "we went into the province of Judea, to the house of the great God" — draws the witnesses to that striking title on pagan lips and to the honest account of the work in progress. The reformed John Gill hears in "the house of the great God" the name the Jews themselves gave their God, and observes that even the heathen had some notion of one supreme God above the inferior deities they worshipped, some of them reckoning that Jehovah, the God of the Jews, was he. He notes too the political undertone: Judea, once a kingdom, is now called a province, having become a part first of the Babylonian and then of the Persian monarchy. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds that in owning him "the great God" the officials spoke a language in which, thus far, the greater part of the Samaritans agreed with them.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes much of the fairness of the report. The officials called the temple the house of the great God, owning the God of Israel to be great and above all gods, as if to say they durst not oppose the building of his house without orders from the king; and they told him truly what was being done. They did not pretend, as an earlier set of accusers had, that the Jews were fortifying the city as men who intended war; they reported simply that the people were rearing a temple, as those who intended worship. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the same title as a solemn tribute to the God of the Jews, one which the decree of Cyrus enables us to understand in so official a document. He pictures Tatnai as dwelling ordinarily at Damascus and coming to Jerusalem deeply impressed by what he saw; the governor gives only a statement of the progress he observed in the temple, and the "walls" he mentions, Ellicott insists, are the walls rising within the temple itself, not the walls of the city — a distinction that matters, since it was the fortifying of the city that had drawn the earlier prohibition.

On the fabric of the building the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds a single vivid touch: "with great stones" tells us they were making a very strong and a very costly building. The witnesses do not divide; they let the verse do its quiet work. An officer of the empire, no friend to the Jews' religion, walks up to the rising house, is moved by its greatness, and writes to his king that the Jews are building for the great God — a report so candid that it does the builders' cause more good than any advocate of their own could have done. The very stones testify, and the governor reports what he cannot help seeing.
9:
Within the letter the officials rehearse for the king the very question they had put on the spot: "Then asked we those elders, and said unto them thus, Who commanded you to build this house, and to make up these walls?" The reformed John Gill identifies the men so questioned as the elders of the province of Judea, its chief men — not a crowd of labourers but the responsible heads of the community, to whom such an inquiry properly belonged. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the officials' purpose in the questioning. They asked the elders who had authorised the work, and further inquired after their names, that they might write to the king the names of the leading men; and on the phrase that describes those men, Keil is precise — it does not mean those who are literally at the head of the rest, but those who act in the capacity of heads, the men bearing responsibility for the undertaking.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supplies the force of the demand as the elders would have felt it. Finding the Jews both busy and prosperous, all hands at work and the building going up apace, the inquisitors pressed their questions: By what authority do you do these things, and who gave you that authority? Who set you to work? Have you that which will bear you out? It is the challenge of lawful power to an enterprise that looks, on its face, unauthorised — and the whole letter is bent on getting that challenge answered from the records at Babylon.

The witnesses do not divide, and the repetition itself is worth noting. The question first asked at the building site is now set down again, word for word, in the report to the king, so that Darius may weigh the very terms of the exchange. There is a fairness in this that the earlier adversaries never showed: the officials do not paraphrase or colour the demand, but lay it before the throne exactly as it was made, together with the answer they received. The elders, for their part, are not treated as culprits caught in a crime but as responsible men asked to show their warrant; and the courteous form of the inquiry — addressed to the elders, seeking names and authority rather than hurling accusations of sedition — is of a piece with the temper of the whole despatch. The builders are asked to justify themselves, and the next verses will show how readily and how nobly they did so, resting their whole case not on their own boldness but on the decree of a king.
10:
The officials tell the king of a second inquiry: "We asked their names also, to certify thee, that we might write the names of the men that were the chief of them." The reformed John Gill takes this of the names of the elders — the men who had set the workmen about the task and bore the direction of it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the purpose plainly: the officials asked after the names in order to write to the king the names of the leading men, the heads of the enterprise, so that the report might be exact and the responsible parties known by name.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, who had already noticed the demand a few verses earlier, presses the point of it. The authorities required the names of the chief promoters of the building, he says, precisely in order to make them responsible — to have on record the men who could be called to account should the work prove to have been undertaken without warrant. There is nothing sinister in this; it is the ordinary caution of an honest official who means to send his king the truth and to name those who must answer for it.

Taken together the witnesses let the verse reveal the temper of the whole proceeding. The officials do not act on rumour, as the earlier accusers had, nor content themselves with vague charges of sedition; they gather names, they record who is responsible, and they promise the king an accurate account. This very thoroughness works, under God, for the builders' good. A cause investigated fairly and reported exactly has nothing to fear from the truth; it is only misrepresentation that the servants of God need dread. The elders, moreover, do not shrink from having their names sent up to the throne — they neither conceal their leaders nor disown their work, but stand ready to be named and, if it come to that, held answerable. And the answer they give, which the next verse records, will turn this cold demand for names into an occasion for one of the noblest confessions in the book: asked who they are, they will reply that they are the servants of the God of heaven and earth. The bookkeeping of a Persian officer becomes the setting for a testimony of faith, and the list of responsible men becomes a roll of those unashamed to own their God.
11:
Asked who they were, the elders answer with a confession the witnesses treat as the heart of the letter: "We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and build the house that was builded these many years ago, which a great king of Israel builded and set up." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke is moved by its candour: "How simple, plain, and ingenuous is this confession!" They were the servants of the God of heaven — and how, then, came they ever into bondage? Why, they provoked the God of heaven, repeatedly sinned against him, and then he gave them into the hands of their enemies. The confession of their dignity and the confession of their fall are spoken in one breath.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the plea the elders make. In calling themselves servants of the God of heaven and earth they answer any charge of faction: the God they worship is not a local deity, so that they cannot be accused of setting up a mere sect in building him a temple; they pay homage to a God on whom the whole creation depends, and who therefore ought to be countenanced by all and hindered by none. And they plead a kind of prescription to the house itself: it was built for the honour of their God by Solomon many ages ago, and is no novel invention of their own; in rebuilding it they are but raising up the foundations of many generations, in the words of Isaiah 58:12. It is the wisdom as well as the duty of kings, Henry adds, to countenance the servants of the God of heaven.

The grammatical-historical witnesses weigh the wording and the spirit. Keil and Delitzsch render the opening more literally still — "We are His, the servants of the God of heaven and earth" — and note that the house they build was raised many years ago, and that a great king of Israel built it and completed it. Charles Ellicott hears in the reply a remarkable act of trust: the elders take the Syrian satrap into their confidence and give, in a few most pathetic words, the whole record of their national honour, their national infidelity, and their national humiliation. Every word of it, he says, is true to the history, while the whole exhibits their deep humility and their holy resolution. The reformed John Gill adds only that they returned this answer to the purpose and in the very manner that follows. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the elders neither boast nor cringe: they own the greatness of the God they serve, they confess without excuse the sin that had cost them their temple, and they rest their case on a title older than any Persian decree — the house that Solomon built for the God of heaven and earth.
12:
The elders go on to confess the ruin of the first temple, and the witnesses read their words as a model of penitent honesty. "After that our fathers had provoked the God of heaven unto wrath, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house, and carried the people away into Babylon." The reformed John Gill points to the theological knot the confession unties: how was it that a people who were the servants of the great God, and a house built for the honour of his name, were not preserved by him but carried into captivity and left desolate? The answer is their own sin — it was for their idolatries that this befell them.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the elders making exactly that point to the king. It was to punish them for their sins, they say, that they were for a time put out of possession of the house — not because the gods of the nations had prevailed against their God, but because they had provoked him; for that he delivered them and their temple into the hand of the king of Babylon. Yet, Henry adds, God never intended thereby to put a final period to their religion: they were only suspended for a time, not deprived for ever, and the very frankness of the confession is meant to show the king that their present building is the resumption of a right that punishment had interrupted but not cancelled.

The grammatical-historical witnesses press the sovereignty the confession implies. Charles Ellicott observes that these words show the people regarded themselves as punished by the sole hand of God — and, more pointedly, they remind the overthrowers of the Chaldean power that they too are no more than instruments of the same divine will; the Persian who now rules Babylon holds his place by the same God who once used Babylon to chasten Judah. Keil and Delitzsch confirm the force of the causal opening — "for this reason, because our fathers provoked the God of heaven" — and note the strength of the verb, that Nebuchadnezzar destroyed this house and carried away its people. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the elders trace their whole calamity to no failure in their God and no strength in Babylon's idols, but to the provocation of their own fathers; and that in owning God's justice in the ruin they also lay hold of his purpose in the restoration. The God who gave them into Nebuchadnezzar's hand for their sin is the God who has now stirred a Persian king to give them back their house — and the empire that destroyed the temple and the empire that rebuilds it are alike his servants.
13:
The elders now come to the ground of their whole case: "But in the first year of Cyrus the king of Babylon the same king Cyrus made a decree to build this house of God." The reformed John Gill fastens on the odd title "Cyrus king of Babylon": Cyrus is so styled, he explains, because this was the first year he was king of Babylon, having lately taken the city, though he had already been king of Persia for many years before. The elders date their warrant, that is, from the very moment the conqueror entered upon the Babylonian throne — the earliest hour at which such a decree could have been given, so that no charge of delay or afterthought could touch it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch tie the sentence back to the opening of the book, where the decree of Cyrus is first recorded in Ezra 1:3, and forward to the account of the temple vessels, comparing Ezra 1:7 and following. They note that the decree named a certain Sheshbazzar, whom Cyrus made governor, or pechah — the same title borne by Zerubbabel in Haggai 1:1 — so that the man entrusted with the commission held a recognised office under the crown. The whole appeal, they observe, presupposes the fuller record already set down at the book's beginning, to which the officials' inquiry now sends the king back.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the strength of the plea. The Jews have the royal decree of Cyrus itself to justify them and to bear them out in what they do; and the decree, Henry stresses, did not merely permit and allow the building — it charged and commanded it. Their enterprise is therefore no act of private presumption but obedience to an imperial order still on the books. The witnesses do not divide, and the shrewdness of the elders' appeal is plain. They rest their right to build not on the sympathy of the present king, which might change, nor on the preaching of their prophets, which a Persian court would not weigh, but on a written decree of Cyrus, the founder of the very empire Darius now governs. To forbid the work would be to overturn the settled act of the throne's own founder; and so the elders, having confessed their sin and owned God's justice, turn the king's attention to the one document that will decide the whole matter — a decree that, they are confident, still lies in the royal archives waiting to be found.
14:
The elders strengthen their case with a detail no court could dismiss — the sacred vessels. "The vessels also of gold and silver of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took out of the temple that was in Jerusalem, and brought them into the temple of Babylon, those did Cyrus the king take out of the temple of Babylon, and they were delivered unto one, whose name was Sheshbazzar, whom he had made governor." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the vessels' whole journey: carried off by Nebuchadnezzar from the temple at Jerusalem into the temple of his own gods at Babylon, they were now taken out again by Cyrus and handed over to Sheshbazzar, whom the king had made governor of Judah.

The reformed John Gill fills in the commission that went with the handing-over. Cyrus made Sheshbazzar governor of Judah and ordered him to carry the vessels to Jerusalem, to build the temple there, and to set them again in it, as the opening chapter of the book had already recorded in Ezra 1:7 and following. The restoration of the vessels and the rebuilding of the house are thus parts of one royal charge, given together and to be fulfilled together; and the very precision of that earlier record, where each article of gold and silver is counted out, makes the elders' present claim impossible to dismiss as invention.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sees the evidential weight of the point. Cyrus delivered the vessels of the temple to a man he entrusted to see them restored to their ancient place and use; and the great advantage of this, Henry observes, is that the Jews had these very vessels to show in confirmation of what they alleged. Their claim to a royal decree was not left to rest on their own word: the gold and silver of the house of God, once plundered and now returned, stood as tangible proof that Cyrus had indeed ordered the temple rebuilt and had put the means of its furnishing into their hands. The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the elders' quiet masterstroke — a decree may be doubted until the archive is searched, but the vessels are already in Jerusalem, visible and countable, silent witnesses that the whole enterprise rests on the settled will of the empire's founder. What Nebuchadnezzar took as spoil, Cyrus restored as duty; and the same vessels that had once measured Judah's humiliation now measure the certainty of her right to build.
15:
The decree's own words are now quoted: "Take these vessels, go, carry them into the temple that is in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be builded in his place." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds a mark of authenticity in the very grammar. The three imperatives that crowd the verse without a connecting word, followed by a fourth, vividly express the feeling of the suppliants as they recall the decree — the eager rush of command heaped on command; and in that breathless syntax, he says, we have another note of historical truth, the accent of a real order remembered and repeated. Keil and Delitzsch read the same construction, rendering it "Take these vessels, go forth, place them in the temple," and noting that the imperatives follow one another in this rapid form of speech without any copula. The closing clause, they observe — "let the house of God be built in its place" — gives the reason for the command to deposit the vessels: they are to be lodged in a house that is itself to be rebuilt upon its former site. The command to house the vessels and the command to raise the temple are thus bound into one, the sacred plate awaiting the very walls that alone could fitly receive it.

That phrase "in his place" is where the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry rests his weight. Cyrus ordered the house to be built in its place, the very same place where it had stood before; and this, Henry judges, the king commanded not only in compassion to the Jews but in a real veneration of their God, for he owned him in his decree, saying, "He is the God." The witnesses do not divide. They gather around a single impression: that the decree quoted here is no vague permission but a detailed and reverent order — the vessels named and consigned, the site fixed, the God of Israel confessed by a pagan king. The elders lay it before Darius exactly as it was given, trusting that its precision will be its own proof; and Ellicott's small grammatical observation joins Henry's theological one to the same end, that a command so particular, so charged with feeling and so respectful of the God whose house it concerns, bears on its face the stamp of truth. Cyrus did not merely tolerate the temple; he decreed it, sited it, and honoured the God for whom it was to rise, so that the very words of the pagan king become a witness for the Jews before his successor.
16:
The elders bring their history down to the present hour: "Then came the same Sheshbazzar, and laid the foundation of the house of God which is in Jerusalem: and since that time even until now hath it been in building, and yet it is not finished." On the identity of Sheshbazzar the witnesses differ. The reformed John Gill argues that the name must mean Zerubbabel, since it was he who laid the foundation of the temple, or at least by whose order it was laid. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke is less sure, taking Sheshbazzar rather for the military officer who conducted the people up from Babylon and had the oversight of the work, though he notes that some understand Ezra by the name. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply follow the man from Babylon to Jerusalem, where he laid the foundations, so that from that time till the present it had been building and was not yet complete.

Keil presses the honesty of the report against a possible objection. The words "from that time until now" do not deny the long stoppage of the work between the last year of Cyrus and the second of Darius; they merely leave unmentioned the circumstance that had caused the delay. Charles Ellicott makes the same observation the pivot of the whole letter: no account is taken of the long interruption, and whether these words are part of the answer the Jewish leaders gave to Tatnai or Tatnai's own statement to Darius, the plain fact of an unfinished house decreed by Cyrus is precisely what demands investigation — for the king must now determine the nature and the validity of that original decree.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry admires most what the elders leave out. The building was begun, they say, as soon as ever they returned, so that they had not forfeited the benefit of the decree by any neglect; it has been in hand ever since, and if it is not finished, that is because they met with opposition. But — and here is the grace of it — they make no complaint of the falsehood and malice of the former governors who had hindered them, though they had cause enough. They render not bitterness for bitterness, nor even just reproach for the most unjust injury, thinking it enough to obtain fair treatment for the future without dragging up old wrongs. In this Henry hears the very temper the apostle enjoins, to give a reason of the hope that is in us with meekness and fear, as 1 Peter 3:15 requires. The witnesses do not finally divide over Sheshbazzar's name; they agree on the thing that matters, that the elders lay before the king a true and generous account — the work begun in obedience, delayed by no fault of their own, and pressed toward a completion that only awaits the king's confirmation of a decree they are sure he will find.
17:
The letter closes with a request that the witnesses find as fair as it is shrewd: "Now therefore, if it seem good to the king, let there be search made in the king's treasure house, which is there at Babylon, whether it be so, that a decree was made of Cyrus the king to build this house of God at Jerusalem, and let the king send his pleasure to us concerning this matter." The reformed John Gill explains what that treasure house was: the place where the archives of the kingdom were kept — the laws, decrees, edicts, and proclamations of state — so that recourse might be had to them as occasion required. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the request in the same terms: the officials ask Darius to cause a search among the royal archives for any decree of Cyrus authorising the temple, and then to communicate his own decision; the "treasure-house" here, they note, is called in the next chapter the "house of the rolls" in Ezra 6:1.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke praises the temper of the whole despatch. He recognises in "the treasure house" a Persian word for a treasury, and he finds in the letter a great deal of good sense and candour: there is nothing of passion or prejudice in it; the officials laid a fair statement before the king without any attempt to prejudice his mind, and gave him just those directions most likely to lead him to the truth and to a correct judgment. And behind the courtesy Clarke sees a higher hand — God was in all this business, giving yet another proof of his continued regard for a disobedient people whom, though he had punished in justice, he had spared in mercy. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the point on which all turned: everything depended on the original decree, which nothing done in the meantime by the usurper could cancel; and the very form of the request seems to imply that it would be found — as indeed it was, for though the original was not recovered at Babylon a copy had been made and preserved elsewhere.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draw the closing moral together. The officials left it to the king to consult the records and then to give what directions he saw fit; and had the Jews' cause been as fairly stated to Artaxerxes in the previous chapter as it was here to Darius, Wesley says, he would hardly have hindered the work — for the people of God could not be persecuted if they were not first belied. Henry says the same with his own edge: God's people could not be baited if they were not dressed up in bears' skins; let but the cause of God and truth be fairly stated and fairly heard, and it will keep its ground. The witnesses do not divide. They close the chapter on a note of quiet confidence — the case honestly reported, the decree certain to be found, and the God who moved a pagan king's pen once already now watching that the record be searched and the truth prevail.
